title: TA8-11845
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the principal claimant), his wife, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their three sons, XXXX, XXXX and XXXX XXXX, all citizens of the Czech Republic, with the exception of XXXX, who is a permanent resident of the Czech Republic but also a citizen of Poland, are seeking refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. (IRPA)
The principal claimant's wife was appointed by the Board to act as the designated representative on behalf of her minor son, Sebastian.

The principal claimant was born in what is now Slovakia. He is ethnically Roma and has experienced discrimination and threats to himself and his family due to his ethnicity. This discrimination, according to the principal claimant, has been at the hands of other citizens, the police and authorities, as well as from overtly racist groups of Neo-Nazis and skinheads who have become more prevalent since the fall of the Communist regime in 1989.

The principal claimant alleges that notwithstanding the money spent to put his children through college, they ended up being waiters and cooks. According to the principal claimant, on one occasion his car was stopped and the police took money from his wallet. When the principal claimant learned of this incident, he took his son to the police station. However, when he told the story and got to the part that it was the police who were the perpetrators, they became very defensive. Reluctantly, they took a report. According to the police they investigated the incident and did not find the person who took his money and punched him, however, he still had to pay a fine.

Both of the principal claimant's sons played soccer at a professional level. According to the principal claimant, when he and his wife went to watch the games, the players made fun of their sons for being gypsies. As well as his colleagues disrespecting them, scouts for national teams now ignored them. Finally, the boys left the team as they realized the abuse would not stop.

In terms of the principal claimant's wife and her workplace, there had been stealing in the restaurant and the employees were told that the tips would go into a fund to pay for the missing items. Finally, the employees accused the woman married to a "gypsy man of being the only one who would steal." This accusation angered the principal claimant's wife who had been with the restaurant prior to the two other women. An argument ensued and one of the women grabbed her by the hair and shook her. The principal claimant as a consequence advised his wife to leave the restaurant as he was angry that she had been subjected to this attack.1

In XXXX 2005, the principal claimant had just finished his shift as a cook. As he was walking to his car, he was approached by four young men dressed like skin heads. An unprovoked attack ensued where the claimant was punched and kicked. The principal claimant was bleeding and did not want his wife to see the injuries. He, therefore, went to his parents' house and pretended to be away for a few weeks. The principal claimant made a denunciation to the police.

The area where the claimants lived became very popular with neo-Nazi/skinhead followers. Out of the eight restaurants and clubs in the area, four outright banned gypsies from entering. Even in the other clubs, although permitted to enter, they would be harassed by neo-Nazi customers who had been contacted specifically to harass them.

On XXXX, 2008 the principal claimant was leaving his apartment with his two sons. His apartment was vandalized with the words "death to Hungarians" which is how they refer to gypsies in the Czech Republic. There was also a Swastika drawn on the door.
The claimants arrived in Canada on XXXX, 2008 and filed claims on June 16, 2008.
The Board finds that the claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identities

The principal claimant is a citizen of the Czech Republic, his wife is a permanent resident of the Czech Republic but also a citizen of Poland, and the children are citizens of the Czech Republic, as per the certified true copies of their passports.2 Determinative Issues
The determinative issue is state protection. State Protection

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The principles, enunciated hereafter, pertain to the case at hand and were accordingly applied. There is a presumption, except in situations where the state is in a complete breakdown, that it is capable of protecting its citizens. A claimant can rebut this presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.3

No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.4

Moreover, local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state on the whole fails to protect its citizens, unless those failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.5 Indeed, if a claimant believes the actions of some police officers are corrupt, the onus is on the claimant to approach other members of the security forces or the authorities.6

Furthermore, the law states that the burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state.7 The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action available.8 Moreover, local failures by the authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.9

While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration,10 the preponderance of recent Federal court decisions has held that the test for a finding of state protection is whether the protection is adequate, rather than effective per se.11 A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken, and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.12

The Board must consider what steps the principal claimant took to seek state protection. The claimants fear "skinheads" and other individuals who hate Romas. According to the principal claimant, because they do not have blue eyes and blonde hair, they are visibly recognized as Romas. However, he acknowledged that since his wife originates from Poland, her visibility is not that of a Roma and his children as a consequence are "mixed."

The principal claimant and his son both testified with regard to the incident which occurred in XXXX 2005.13 The principal claimant testified that there was no investigation in this regard when a police officer himself was the perpetrator, whereas the foregoing paragraph indicates that there was, in fact, an investigation. At the second sitting, the claimant's son, XXXX, confirmed that he had received a letter indicating that there had been an investigation, he had to pay a fine, and the perpetrator was not located. XXXX was asked the whereabouts of this letter, to which he responded that it probably stayed in the house or was thrown out. He had not followed up on this letter, because according to him, he had lost his strength at this point.

The XXXX 2005 incident, in which the principal claimant was approached by four young men and the victim of an unprovoked attack, was reported to the police. However, according to the principal claimant although he attempted to obtain a copy of this report, he was told it did not exist.

In XXXX 2007, the principal claimant's wife decided to leave her place of employment after a dispute, in which she was attacked and accused of stealing money. She chose, at the recommendation of her husband, to resign.14 However, she did not report the matter to the police. When asked why she did not, she responded "I did not go."

The XXXX, 2008 incident, which according to the claimants was the pivotal point at which they decided to come to Canada, was reported to the police.15 Moreover, although the claimants submitted photographs of this incident, they acknowledged that the police themselves took photos. This occurred just weeks before their departure. The principal claimant was asked if he was aware of the outcome of any investigation in this regard. He was not aware and acknowledged that he had not pursued the matter.

The Board concludes that with the exception of one incident, the XXXX 2005 incident, the police pursued investigation stemming from the reports. In the first instance, they were unable to locate the perpetrator and the principal claimant did not pursue the matter further.
The principal claimant's wife chose to leave the restaurant of her own accord, and chose not to report the matter to the police.

The incident, which according to the principal claimant, was the reason for the claimants' departure in 2008 was reported to the police, they took photographs, however the claimants are unaware of the results of this investigation.
In totality, the claimants have not provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect them. Counsel's Submissions

Documentary evidence indicates that the Czech Republic is a multiparty parliamentary democracy with a population of approximately 10.2 million. Legislative authority is vested in the bicameral parliament, consisting of a Chamber of Deputies and Senate.

The National police are responsible for enforcing the law and maintaining public order. While law enforcement bodies were generally effective, corruption remained a problem. The Interior Ministry oversees police actions and is responsible for investigating allegations of police misconduct.
The laws provide for the right to a fair trial, and the independent judiciary generally enforced this right. Defendants enjoy a presumption of innocence and trials are public.

According to Amnesty International, Roma continued to suffer discrimination from public officials and private individuals in education, housing, health and employment. Localities with marginalized Romani communities became targets of far-right groups; public officials continued to use racist language against the Roma.

However, by law, police must respond to all distress calls and notify parties of the outcome of their complaints. Every individual who files a complaint has the right to a copy of their police report. When asked about police protection measures against discrimination and racially motivated violence, governmental interlocutors pointed to Roma Police Assistants, Minority Liaison Officers, and the Ministry of the Interior's Anti-Extremism Strategy. In addition, the Ministry of the Interior's Strategy on Policing Minorities was passed on 9 April 2008 under government Resolution No. 384. The main objectives of this strategy include training on policing minority communities, efforts to employ minorities into the police force, researching crime in socially excluded localities, as well as maintaining the MLO and RPA initiatives.16

Governmental and NGO interlocutors varied in their assessment of police relations with Roma. However, e.g. in Brno, it was indicated that police are frequently called to the scene of a conflict only to be told that the situation has been resolved. Similarly, Diapa noted that Roma often refuse to cooperate in follow-up investigations to crimes they report, subsequently leading to cases being dropped. However several NGO and academic interlocutors commented that the police generally have a negative view of Roma that sometimes includes discriminatory or disrespectful attitudes.

The Ombudsman seeks to investigate allegations of public sector mistreatment on the basis of a complaint or on his or her own initiative. The Ombudsman's office has jurisdiction covering a wide range of government ministries, as well as municipal and administrative authorities performing state functions. Since the first Ombudsman was appointed in 2000, he has received no formal complaints against the state police. However, he has received unofficial reports from NGOs and individuals alleging that they were bullied by state police, however, he could not act in the absence of formal complaints.

There are NGOs who are active and provide a range of services and activities for Roma. They monitor cases of private sector discrimination and bring such cases to court, provide legal assistance, monitor and speak out against neo-Nazi groups.

DROM is a Brno-based NGO that carries out a wide range of activities in Romani communities, including social and legal services, child care, education and recreational activities. IQ Roma Servis is a Brno-based NGO that provides community and social field work, free counseling and legal services together with employment support for Roma clients in socially excluded localities. Other organizations include Socioklub, The Association of the Romanies in Moravia, Asvule Prava, the League of Human Rights etc.

The Roma Police Assistant (RPA) program was created in 2003 with seed money from the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MPSV).17 RPAs are now mainly funded by municipalities via National government grants. RPA duties include establishing contact between Roma and the police, accompanying Romani victims of crime who wish to file a police report, educating victims on their legal rights and responsibilities, helping police investigate unreported crime, and assisting in the provision of social services in socially excluded localities. While no formal evaluations of their effectiveness have been carried out, police and municipalities believed RPAs to be efficient and valuable. Several NGO interlocutors also identified the existence of the RPA program as a sign of progress and two interlocutors claimed that RPAs have increased Romani trust in the police.

There is nothing in the documentation before the Board to suggest that the Czech Republic is in a state of complete breakdown. The onus is on the claimant to show that he or she has exhausted all courses of action available.18 The claimants have not met that burden. They have not provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect them.

While acknowledging that discrimination against the Roma remains a problem, the preponderance of the documentary evidence indicates that the Czech Republic government is making very serious efforts to provide protection to the Roma whether as victims of hate crime, or assisting them in obtaining inclusion into Czech society.

For the foregoing reasons, the Board finds that there is not a serious possibility that the principal claimant would be subject to persecution, or that, on a balance of probabilities, his removal to the Czech Republic would subject him personally to a risk to his life, a risk of unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture. Since all claims are based on the fears of the principal claimant, they are also found not to be in need of protection.

Accordingly, all claims are rejected.
